passage: Chen ate lunch on the steps behind the gym because the cafeteria felt like a stage. Three boys had started calling him "ghost", and by now he believed nobody at school wanted him around. In the library, Oskar from the chess club slid a spare board across the table. "Black or white?" Chen shrugged, then played. On the walk home he heard himself say, quietly, "They are being mean to me." Oskar only nodded and said his sister had been teased once too. The next week Chen told the chess teacher what was happening, and the steps behind the gym were no longer the only place he could eat.

qa.q: Where did Chen eat lunch?
qa.a: He ate lunch on the steps behind the gym.

qa.q: How did Chen feel after the boys started calling him "ghost"?
qa.a: Chen felt lonely and unwanted; he believed nobody at school wanted him around and ate lunch on the steps behind the gym instead of the cafeteria.

qa.q: What helped Chen feel less alone, and what did he do next?
qa.a: A boy from the chess club offered him a game, and Chen said out loud that they were being mean to him and then told the chess teacher.

qa.q: What might Oskar be thinking when he nods and mentions his sister was teased?
qa.a: Oskar may want Chen to know he is not the only one it has happened to and that Oskar understands, which makes him a safe friend.

grounding: A bullied child feels nobody wants him, then finds one safe friend and a club and says it aloud.

passage: Leila's phone buzzed during dinner, and the class group chat was full of laughing faces under a photo of her mid-sneeze, mouth wide open. Her cheeks burned. She typed "not funny!!" and deleted it, then typed something meaner and deleted that too. Her thumbs shook. Instead she took a screenshot and put the phone face down. Her older sister Elif saw her pushing peas around the plate. "What happened?" Elif asked. Leila showed her. Elif did not laugh. "Thank you for showing me. Tomorrow we take this to your teacher, and we keep the screenshot." Leila breathed out slowly. It still hurt, but it was no longer only hers to carry.

qa.q: What did Leila do with the photo instead of replying?
qa.a: She took a screenshot and put the phone face down.

qa.q: Why did Leila type messages and then delete them?
qa.a: She was hurt and angry and part of her wanted to snap back, but she seemed to sense that an angry reply would not help.

qa.q: What would you advise Leila to do with the screenshot?
qa.a: She should keep it safe and show it to her teacher with Elif's help, rather than answering the group in anger.

qa.q: How might Elif feel on seeing the photo?
qa.a: Elif was probably upset for her sister but stayed calm, since she did not laugh, thanked Leila for showing her and planned to go to the teacher.

grounding: A child is laughed at in a class chat, does not reply in anger, saves the screenshot and tells family and teacher.

passage: Uday here. I was standing by the water cooler when a boy from the other class started tapping Harsha's head with a ruler again. Harsha had been quiet for weeks, and I expected him to freeze. Instead he looked straight at the boy and said, "Stop that. I don't like it." His voice wobbled a little, but it did not shout. Then he picked up his bottle and walked off towards the staff room. I heard later that he had told the class teacher earlier that week and had practised those words with them. I can't say if he was scared inside. The ruler boy just stood there with his mouth open, and that afternoon the class teacher had a word with him.

qa.q: What did Harsha say to the boy with the ruler?
qa.a: He said, "Stop that. I don't like it."

qa.q: What might Harsha have been feeling as he spoke, judging by his wobbling voice?
qa.a: He was probably nervous, but Uday cannot be sure; the wobble alongside steady words suggests he was brave even though he may have been afraid.

qa.q: What should happen if the boy keeps teasing Harsha even after he says stop?
qa.a: Harsha should not handle it alone; adults like the class teacher need to step in, as the teacher already did that afternoon.

qa.q: How might the ruler boy have felt when Harsha spoke up?
qa.a: He was probably taken by surprise, since he stood there with his mouth open and had expected Harsha to freeze.

grounding: A classmate watches a child who practised a calm, firm voice say stop and leave, with adults still involved.

passage: With ten minutes left before the picnic bus left, Kashish grabbed Sachin's cap and tossed it between two friends, and everyone laughed. He liked that sound; it made him feel tall. Sachin stood by the bus door and said nothing, his eyes on his shoes, his lip pressed white. For a moment Kashish really saw that look, and remembered his elder brother doing the same to him at home while the family watched. His laugh dried up. The teacher was calling out names and time was short, but Kashish walked over, held out the cap and said, "Sorry. That wasn't funny." Sachin took it without a word. It was not enough, and Kashish knew it.

qa.q: What did Kashish do with Sachin's cap?
qa.a: He tossed it between two friends.

qa.q: Why did Kashish's laugh dry up after he looked at Sachin?
qa.a: He saw the hurt in Sachin's face and it reminded him of how his elder brother treated him at home, so the teasing no longer made him feel big.

qa.q: What made Kashish's apology a step in the right direction, and what more might he do?
qa.a: He stopped, returned the cap and said sorry plainly; he could also stay kinder from now on and ask himself why he wanted to feel big.

qa.q: How might Sachin see the apology?
qa.a: Sachin took the cap without a word, so he may still feel hurt or unsure it is real; an apology starts repair but does not fix things at once.

grounding: A child who teases a quieter boy for laughs notices his hurt, stops and apologises.

passage: Emeka strolled down the corridor, ready to make his usual joke about Wei's glasses, and Wei flinched. His shoulders jumped up and his books rose against his chest like a shield. Emeka's grin faltered. He had expected to feel big; instead his stomach turned. Behind him his friends were waiting for the punchline. "It's just a joke," he began, and heard how false it sounded. Wei had already backed against the lockers. So Emeka dropped his voice. "Sorry, Wei. I'm not going to say it. I shouldn't have said it before, either." Wei only looked at him, unsure. Emeka walked away, red in the face.

qa.q: Where was Wei standing when Emeka apologised?
qa.a: Wei had already backed against the lockers.

qa.q: What was Emeka feeling when he saw Wei flinch?
qa.a: His grin faltered and his stomach turned, so he felt uncomfortable and ashamed instead of the big feeling he expected.

qa.q: What did Emeka's apology get right, and what might he still need to do?
qa.a: He stopped, admitted he should not have said it before, and did not call it a joke; he may need to keep his word over the coming days so Wei can feel safe.

qa.q: How might Wei see Emeka's apology?
qa.a: Wei looked unsure, which suggests he may not trust it yet after being teased, and he may need time to see that Emeka means it.

grounding: A teaser sees the target's fear, feels uncomfortable instead of proud, and stops and says sorry.

passage: Monday: Behind the cricket nets, Ira watched three older boys mock a Class 4 boy's lunchbox. They roared with laughter, and Ira thought, that is what cool looks like. Thursday: At the water tap, Ira copied their sneering voice to the same younger boy. A few in his row chuckled, but the boy's eyes filled and Ira felt something sour in his throat. Next Tuesday: His neighbour Pema asked him to join the drawing corner at lunch. Nobody there laughed at anyone. Ira made a lopsided dragon, and Pema only said, "Good tail." He noticed he had not needed to be loud to belong.

qa.q: What did Ira make in the drawing corner?
qa.a: He made a lopsided dragon.

qa.q: How did Ira feel after copying the older boys at the water tap?
qa.a: Ira felt guilty and uneasy: the younger boy's eyes filled and Ira felt something sour in his throat, even though a few in his row chuckled.

qa.q: What made the drawing corner a better place for Ira to belong?
qa.a: Nobody laughed at anyone there and Pema simply praised the dragon's tail, so Ira could belong without being loud or picking a victim.

qa.q: How might the Class 4 boy have felt at the water tap?
qa.a: He was probably hurt and embarrassed, since his eyes filled when Ira copied the sneering voice.

grounding: A child copies older boys' teasing to seem cool, feels the cost, and finds belonging in a kinder group.

passage: The phone rang while the pressure cooker whistled, and Zeenat heard her mother say, "Yes, Ma'am... yes, I will speak to her." Dilnaz put the phone down and switched off the stove. Her face was quiet, which was worse than shouting. "The teacher says you called Sana names and left her out of the game." Zeenat's face went hot. "She started it," she began, then stopped, because it was not true. She wanted to slip under the bed. Dilnaz waited. At last Zeenat whispered, "I was mean." They sat on the kitchen floor while the dal cooled, and Dilnaz asked what Zeenat could say to Sana in the morning.

qa.q: What did the teacher say Zeenat did to Sana?
qa.a: The teacher said Zeenat called Sana names and left her out of the game.

qa.q: Why did Zeenat start to say "She started it" and then stop?
qa.a: She felt hot with shame and wanted to blame Sana, but she knew it was not true, so she stopped and owned what she had done.

qa.q: What would be a good way for Zeenat to repair things with Sana?
qa.a: She could say a sincere sorry to Sana without excuses or blame, and ask how to do better, as Dilnaz's question about the morning invites.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz be feeling as she waits in silence?
qa.a: Dilnaz is probably disappointed and worried, yet she stays calm and gives Zeenat room to be honest instead of shouting.

grounding: A child told off after bullying feels hot with shame, resists blaming the victim, and admits it.

passage: With five minutes left before the bell, Jahnavi Ma'am called Akash into the corridor and asked him quietly what had happened at the tap with Nikhil. She did not shout. Akash's first thought was to say Nikhil had bumped him. The words were ready. But her calm, waiting face made the lie feel heavy in his mouth. "I pushed him," he said. "I was annoyed about the cricket team." She asked what was really bothering him, and he admitted he had been feeling left out. "Thank you for telling me the truth," she said. They agreed he would talk to Nikhil before the bell and ask what he needed. Akash's chest felt lighter than he expected.

qa.q: What did Akash say when the teacher asked what had happened at the tap?
qa.a: He said, "I pushed him."

qa.q: Why did the lie feel heavy in Akash's mouth?
qa.a: The teacher's calm, waiting face made lying feel worse than owning up, so he chose to be honest and it felt lighter.

qa.q: What steps in this scene helped Akash repair the harm?
qa.a: He admitted the push, agreed to talk to Nikhil and ask what he needed, and looked at what he had really been feeling.

qa.q: How might Nikhil see Akash coming to talk to him?
qa.a: Nikhil may be surprised or wary at first, but an honest apology that asks what he needs gives him a chance to feel respected.

grounding: A teacher calmly asks a child who pushed another, and the child owns it and plans to repair it.

passage: Thursday night. Today Kabir put Hemant's bag on the roof of the cycle shed and everyone laughed. I laughed too, really loud, so nobody would think I was boring. Hemant looked straight at me for one second. Now my stomach feels weird and I couldn't finish dinner. I keep thinking I should have said something. I did not mean it, but I did laugh, and that is the thing. Tomorrow I will say sorry to Hemant first thing, before class. And if Kabir does something like that again, I won't laugh. I will walk away or stand next to Hemant. No excuses in my head this time. -- Raghav

qa.q: Where did Kabir put Hemant's bag?
qa.a: Kabir put it on the roof of the cycle shed.

qa.q: Why does Raghav feel sick tonight?
qa.a: Raghav laughed along with the others and remembers Hemant's look, so guilt is at work, and the plan to apologise shows Raghav's conscience is working.

qa.q: What does Raghav plan to do next, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Raghav plans to say sorry to Hemant first thing tomorrow and not laugh if it happens again, which turns guilt into action instead of excuses.

qa.q: How might Hemant have felt when looking at Raghav during the laughing?
qa.a: Hemant may have felt hurt and let down that a friend was laughing, since Hemant looked straight at Raghav for one second.

grounding: A child who laughed along at someone feels guilt, plans an apology and to refuse next time.

passage: Dear diary, today in front of the whole class I called Siddharth "Pimple", and everyone laughed. He went quiet and stared at his shoes. It did not feel as good as I thought it would. I know why I do it. I am the shortest boy in Class 6, and every day I wait for someone to start on me. So I go first, and then nobody can. But tonight I keep thinking about Siddharth's face. Maybe I could sit with Ravi and the chess boys instead. They don't do this stuff. And maybe I can stop hating my height so much. -- Manoj

qa.q: What did Manoj call Siddharth in front of the class?
qa.a: He called him "Pimple".

qa.q: Why does Manoj tease others about their looks before anyone can tease him?
qa.a: He is scared of being teased about being the shortest, so he strikes first, hoping that way nobody can start on him.

qa.q: What could Manoj try instead of attacking first?
qa.a: He could sit with kinder friends, such as the chess boys, and work on feeling okay about himself rather than picking on others.

qa.q: How might Siddharth have felt when the class laughed?
qa.a: Siddharth probably felt embarrassed and hurt, since he went quiet and stared at his shoes.

grounding: A child who teases others about their looks because he dreads being teased sees the pattern and plans a kinder way.
